These skills package procedural knowledge that can be reused across recurring classes of tasks. As skill libraries grow, however, explicitly exposing every available skill in the context becomes increasingly impractical. Recent work therefore shifts toward Skill Retrieval Augmentation (SRA), where skills must be retrieved and loaded from a largescale skill corpora (Su et al., 2026) (Figure 1). As interaction histories grow, retaining all prior examples for checking each update also makes continual adaptation increasingly expensive. This creates a need for a routing mechanism whose applicability criteria are explicit and editable, but whose updates are efficiencly constrained by prior experience and independently checked for generalization. These problems of controlling regressions while bounding used experience serve as the motivation for our approach. We introduce RouterBSI, a recursive selfimproving algorithm for skill routing in a black-box setting called RouterBSI. It refines task applicability predicates using Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) with bounded replay to minimize errors on seen tasks and a held-out validation gate to reduce regressions on unseen tasks. The router evaluates predicates for top-k retrieved skills then selects skills if the task satisfies their respective predicate. RouterBSI improves its cold-start top-5 recall of required skills by an average of 24.9% across different retrievers on tasks from TheoremQA, LogicBench, ToolQA, MedCalc-Bench, CHAMP, and BigCodeBench sharing a 26k skill corpus. On average, it retains 90.5% of the required skills in top 5 from the top 50 skills retrieved. Its top-5 recall is 75.5%, with relative recall improvements over baselines averaging 7.9% to 33.6% across retrievers. Our contributions are: • We propose RouterBSI, a non-parametric skillrouting framework that evaluates explicit applicability predicates over retrieved candidates, making routing criteria interpretable and directly editable without updating the underlying language model. • We develop a recursive self-improvement procedure that refines predicates from routing failures, selects updates through minimum Bayes risk over a bounded replay of relevant and irrelevant tasks, and rejects updates with higher held-out validation error than the cold-start predicate. • We evaluate RouterBSI on six SRA-Bench datasets with a shared 26K-skill corpus, achieving the highest aggregate nDCG@10 and Hit@1 among evaluated methods while ablations establish the contributions of replay and validation. Related Works 2.1 Non-Parametric Routing Optimization Non-parametric routing optimization updates external routing state from task feedback while keeping model weights fixed. Experience-based methods revise memories and procedures, but revisions can undo earlier improvements (Wang et al., 2025b; Ouyang et al., 2026; Guo et al., 2024). Structural methods evolve skill relationships, but graph expansions can introduce many irrelevant skills, reducing precision or exceeding context limits (Zhang et al., 2025; Bai et al., 2026). Gated updates limit regressions through surrogate objectives or rollback criteria but don’t directly minimizing routing error on seen tasks (Mi et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). Similar to our approach, JTPRO evaluates candidates on sampled training minibatches and held-out validation but does not provide bounded experience management for online adaptation (Ghoshal et al., 2026). Retaining earlier routing corrections while bounding experience and evaluation costs remains a challenge. RouterBSI ensures non-decreasing empirical error on the retained set while bounding replay evaluation costs. A held-out gate additionally rejects updates that regress validation performance below the cold-start performance. 2.2 Parametric Routing Optimization Parametric routing optimization updates model weights using supervision, preferences, or execution feedback. Learned retrievers and rerankers score relevance or utility of skill for task (Qin et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026), while direct selectors predict which capability to invoke or whether invocation is needed (Wang et al., 2025a; Qian et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a). Reinforcementlearning policies optimize skill routing from downstream rewards (Wang et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026). These approaches require large training data and encode routing criteria implicitly in model weights. RouterBSI keeps the model fixed and refines natural-language applicability predicates that humans can inspect and edit.

We evaluate skill routing and downstream performance conditioned on the selected skills. For skill routing, we report Recall@k and nDCG@k. The retrievers include sparse and dense retrievers (Su et al., 2026) and SkillSight, a hybrid retriever. They are trained on training split and frozen on validation and test splits. LLM Select is a static router, and LLM Direct and LLM Oracle are downstream performance baselines representing without skills and with ground-truth skill set, respectively (Su et al., 2026). The non-parametric optimization baselines are SkillDag and Skill-Pro (Mi et al., 2026; Bai et al., 2026). RouterBSIinit and RouterBSI refer to the cold-start and final iteration performance. RouterBSIstrict selects skills only when their predicate evaluates to true. RouterBSItopk are the top k skills using the sum of their predicate label and the retrieval score. 5.5 Implementation Details. The retrievers use either pretrained embedding models and/or lexical matching, so they do not require training. Candidate skills are retrieved from the shared external skill corpus in response to the input query. The skill routing baselines are conditioned on the top 50 retrieved skills and use some optimization method to improve performance. The exception is SkillDAG where it first retrieves top 5 skills then expands them until reaching top k. Its skills are ranked based on graph depth from top 5 retrieved skills and retrieval score. SkillSight is the default retriever. Qwen3.5-4B is the default model used in our experiments. The non-parametric baselines, including ours, do not output a continuous score like rerankers, so we rank them by the sum of their binary label and the retrieval score, where 1 is the label for selected skills and 0 otherwise. We use a temperature of 1 for proposing candidate predicates and 0 for evaluating predicates and downstream performance. RouterBSI is optimized for 10 iterations. In downstream tasks, we use k = 5 skills for SkillRouter and RouterBSItopk, and we set k = 10 for SkillDAG because k = 5 would match the retriever’s performance. Combining MBR with the held-out gate further improved final performance on unseen test tasks, increasing F1 by 3.28% and nDCG@1 by 4.71% to 0.724 compared with MBR alone. Relative to each configuration’s own initialization, disabling both only increases F1 and nDCG@1 by 21.0% and 6.8% which is much lower than the 100.9% and 38.8% increase when both are enabled. This supports empirical update selection without implying that unchecked updates invariably worsen performance. With both components enabled, diminishing returns appeared around iteration 5, by which point 96.5% of the final F1 gain and 93.0% of the final net nDCG@1 gain had accrued. Later iterations added only 0.011 F1 and 0.014 nDCG@1, indicating an approximate plateau. This suggest diminishing opportunities for useful predicate refinement on the plateau: early iterations correct broad, frequent routing errors, while later iterations encounter harder or less common cases. 7.2 Performance and Token Usage Tradeoff of MBR Replay and Held-out Gate Figure 6 demonstrates that combining replay and the gate provides the strongest final routing performance, while MBR alone reduces token usage by 10.8% at the cost of a 7.7% relative decrease in nDCG@1 compared with using both. Stronger backbones improve initialization, while optimization brings smaller model Qwen3.5 4B close to the optimized performance of GPT-OSS 120B. RouterBSI achieves the strongest average routing performance among evaluated methods and preserves more required skills as the selection budget decreases. Ablations support the complementary contributions of replay and validation and show improvements across model backbones. These findings demonstrate the value of editable predicates and feedback-driven skill routing. Future work can connect skills based on dependencies to improve skill routing performance or jointly optimize predicates and skills to improve downstream performance. Limitations Our approach has three limitations. First, training is computationally expensive, although optimization converges on the training data and improves overall routing performance. Second, we do not provide a protocol for determining which skills a task requires. The method therefore relies on human annotations or an external labeling mechanism, making optimization dependent on the availability and accuracy of these labels. Third, we keep the predicate checker’s instructions fixed, even though errors in interpreting predicates can lead to incorrect skill selections. Our algorithm indirectly improves checking performance by generating and selecting predicate formulations that the checker evaluates more accurately against labeled tasks; however, it does not directly address weaknesses in the checker’s instructions. Ethical Considerations Our experiments reuse existing SRA-Bench tasks, annotations, and skill content, which may contain errors, biases, or harmful instructions. Reuse should respect dataset, skill, and model licenses, while sensitive task data require appropriate access controls and retention policies, particularly when using external model services. Incorrect predicate judgments can omit required skills or admit inappropriate ones, propagating errors to downstream decisions. Bounded replay and held-out validation assess routing behavior rather than factual correctness, fairness, or safety. Results on MedCalc-Bench do not establish clinical validity or suitability for patient care; high-stakes applications require domain-specific validation and qualified human oversight. Retrieved instructions and generated code should be treated as untrusted content, with permission controls and isolated execution before use. Our approach has three limitations. First, training
495
is computationally expensive, although optimiza-
496
tion converges on the training data and improves

498

504

rect skill selections. Our algorithm indirectly im-

cess controls and retention policies, particularly

522

523

A Routing and Improvement Procedure A.1 Initialization and Online Routing We initialize one predicate psi for every skill s ∈S from its public name, description, and body. The generator receives no task labels. It produces one reusable applicability statement of at most l characters. This limit also applies to subsequent replacements. Compound statements may contain AND, OR, and NOT, but they are evaluated as one predicate. The improvement procedure neither adds predicates nor decomposes them into separately evaluated clauses. For a task q, we retrieve S@k and evaluate each retrieved predicate against the public task text. Strict routing returns Pq = {s ∈S@k : ps(q) = True}. The evaluator receives only the task and predicate, not Gq, a reference answer, or the skill body. During training, required-skill annotations identify the failure set Fq = ((Gq ∩S@k) \ Pq) ∪(Pq \ Gq). A required skill outside S@k is a retrieval miss and does not trigger a predicate repair. We traverse the training tasks in their fixed split order for each iteration. For one task, repairs to distinct failed skills can execute in parallel; all results are joined before committing them in skillidentifier order. The next task is routed with the resulting predicates. This preserves sequential online updates across tasks while allowing parallel evaluator calls. For a ranked rather than strictly filtered output, the implementation orders candidates lexicographically by predicate label, retrieval score, and original retrieval order, placing true labels first. This is the operational interpretation of the label-based prioritization in the main text; it is not an unnormalized arithmetic sum for arbitrary retrieval scores. For SkillSight, the exposed score is 1/j at retrieval rank j ≥1, so adding a binary label yields the same selected-first ordering. A fixed-size top-k output may therefore include false-labelled candidates, unlike strict routing. A.2 Bounded Replay Construction For each skill, we retain two training-history buckets, H+ s and H− s , containing at most N relevant and N irrelevant tasks. Membership is determined by s ∈Gq. Before routing, each newly seen training task is registered once in a global seen-task history. After routing, we materialize the bounded buckets for every retrieved or required catalog skill in sorted skill-identifier order, including skills without a routing error. A newly materialized bucket replays the already-seen history; an existing bucket processes the new history entries. Only these perskill buckets are capacity-limited, not the global history used for lazy materialization. A bucket is filled until it reaches N entries. Thereafter, every newly seen task of that category replaces a uniformly selected existing slot. This is uniform slot replacement, not reservoir sampling: the new task is always inserted. A seeded randomnumber generator shared across buckets and the deterministic materialization order determine the replacements. Repeated visits to a task in later iterations do not insert it again. When repairing the failure on q, the effective replay set is Rs = H+ s ∪H− s ∪{q}, with duplicate task identifiers removed. Thus the historical bounds are |H+ s |, |H− s | ≤N, while the current-inclusive set can have 2N + 1 tasks if q is no longer cached. The bounds in the main replay description apply to the retained history; the current failed task is always included in the implemented decision. The proposal prompt receives the current task and its relevance label, plus up to the first three entries from each bucket, with their existing predicate judgments. Candidate scoring uses the entire effective replay set, not just these prompt examples. Bucket order, rather than a new random sample, determines the displayed examples. A.3 Candidate Admission and Minimum-Risk Selection For a failed predicate pf, we request Mp distinct replacement strings. Each must be a declarative applicability statement within the shared length limit, distinct from pf, and must preserve the singlepredicate structure. The unchanged pf is evaluated separately rather than requested as a generated candidate.

C Benchmark and Skill Corpus Details C.1 Task Filtering and Split Construction We use the six task collections distributed with SRA-Bench (Su et al., 2026). Table 3 gives the exact task and gold-skill counts after filtering. Starting from 5,400 annotated instances, we remove any task whose required set contains a skill occurring in fewer than three remaining tasks. We recompute skill frequencies and repeat this operation until no such task remains. Filtering removes whole tasks rather than individual labels from a multi-skill task. This leaves 4,987 tasks associated with 306 distinct gold skills; 413 tasks are excluded. We target a global train/validation/test allocation of 70%/15%/15%, yielding 3,491/748/748 tasks. A constrained allocation assigns tasks while ensuring that every retained skill occurs in all three partitions. For each skill, split counts lie within floor/ceiling bounds around the target proportions, clipped to leave at least one occurrence in each partition. The allocation minimizes normalized deviations from the target proportions for both skills and datasets, and uses split seed 20260908 to order task identifiers within each dataset–gold-set group. The constraints can shift an individual dataset away from the global proportions, particularly when many skills have few examples; the exact counts therefore take precedence over an assumed per-dataset ratio. Task identifiers are disjoint across partitions, but the skill vocabulary is deliberately shared: each partition contains all 306 retained gold skills. The evaluation consequently measures generalization to held-out tasks involving represented skills, rather than to entirely unseen skills. C.2 Required-Skill Labels and Task Types Each instance has a task identifier and a nonempty annotated set of required skill identifiers. We use these released associations as the routing targets, preserving all labels of a retained task. TheoremQA concerns theorem application, LogicBench logical reasoning, ToolQA tool-use workflows, MedCalc- Bench medical calculators, CHAMP mathematical concepts, and BigCodeBench software-library use. All retained TheoremQA, LogicBench, ToolQA, and MedCalc-Bench tasks have exactly one annotated required skill. BigCodeBench and CHAMP also test recovery of multiple required skills. All 1,059 retained BigCodeBench tasks have multiple labels. CHAMP contains 90 single-skill and 78 multi-skill tasks. Across the six collections, the retained data contain 6,932 task–skill annotation occurrences, distinct from the 306 unique skills. The test split contains 1,097 annotation occurrences over 748 tasks: 608 tasks have one required skill and 140 have multiple required skills. The latter comprise all 123 BigCodeBench test tasks and 17 of the 26 CHAMP test tasks. Big- CodeBench test tasks require between two and six annotated skills; CHAMP test tasks require between one and four. Routing recall uses the entire annotated required set as its denominator, so recovering one relevant skill does not necessarily recover all requirements of a multi-skill task. For annotation-based precision and F1, selected skills outside this set count as false positives. This convention defines the evaluation target; it does not imply that an unannotated skill cannot help a downstream agent. We do not replace a multi-skill target with a single representative label. C.3 Shared Skill Corpus and Data Access The shared SRA-Bench retrieval corpus contains 26,262 distinct skill identifiers: 636 gold skills associated with the unfiltered task collections and 25,626 web-collected distractors (Su et al., 2026). A skill record provides a name, description, and content, which may include instructions, formulas, workflows, or code. All annotated skill identifiers in the task collections resolve to records in this corpus. Filtering the task splits reduces the evaluated gold vocabulary to 306 skills; it does not reduce the shared retrieval corpus to those skills. The SRA-Bench package is publicly available as WeihangSu/SRA-Bench on Hugging Face, with the accompanying SR-Agents toolkit. The distributed dataset metadata specifies the MIT license.
